g.text: Two offsets, not one - and consumers may only read the lower of them
Conflating the log end offset with the high watermark is the most common source of confusion here, and it is a correctness bug.
Leader and followers, at differing lag
LEADER
log end offset = 105
follower A
at 104
follower B
at 103 <- sets the high watermark
follower C
at 101 -> EVICTED from the ISR
HIGH WATERMARK = 103
LOG END = 105
consumers may read this far
invisible
The failure restricting reads to the high watermark prevents
1. consumer reads 105
past the HW, if allowed
2. processes + commits
acts on it - charges a card
3. leader dies
before 104-105 reach anyone
4. follower at 103 elected
becomes the new leader
5. 104 and 105 exist NOWHERE
and 104/105 get REASSIGNED
The consumer has processed and committed a message the system now says was never written - and if it was 'charge this card',
that has already happened and is unrecoverable from the log. Worse, offsets 104 and 105 will be REASSIGNED to different
future messages, so the log's history has changed underneath every consumer tracking positions.
Restricting reads to the high watermark means a consumer can NEVER observe a message that might later vanish. The HW is
exactly the boundary of 'this message survives any single-leader failure' - which is also why consumers read from the leader
and not a follower: a follower's view of the HW lags by one fetch round trip.
Why the ISR exists: both obvious designs are bad
wait for ALL replicas
one slow replica makes the partition UNAVAILABLE
wait for a FIXED quorum (2 of 3)
cannot tell '5ms behind' from 'dead for an hour'
the ISR: a DYNAMIC quorum
ack when everyone CURRENTLY keeping up has it
Note the ISR is defined in TIME, not message count. A count-based threshold fails under bursty load: a 10x spike pushes every
follower past it through no fault of their own, collapsing the ISR to just the leader and silently destroying the durability
guarantee at exactly the moment load is highest.
replication.factor = 3 min.insync.replicas = 2 acks = all
ISR of 3 -> succeed. ISR of 2 -> succeed. ISR of 1 -> WRITES FAIL
That last line is the design deliberately choosing UNAVAILABILITY over silent
durability loss - and it is the most commonly mis-set option in real deployments.
acks=all alone gives a guarantee that quietly evaporates precisely when the cluster
is unhealthy, because 'all' can shrink to one.
